content.text:
Yes. In the U.S., there are several teaching fields where schools often report **not enough qualified people trying to teach**—but it depends a lot on **state, district, grade level, and certification area**.

The biggest recurring shortage areas are:

1. **Special education**  
   This is usually the most severe and widespread shortage. In 2024–25 data, special education was reported as a shortage area in **45 states**. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))

2. **Science**  
   Especially **physics, chemistry, and sometimes middle/high-school general science**. Science was reported as a shortage area in **41 states** for 2024–25. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))

3. **Mathematics**  
   High-school and middle-school math are perennial shortage areas. Math was reported as a shortage area in **40 states** for 2024–25. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))

4. **World languages / foreign languages**  
   Many districts struggle to find teachers for Spanish, French, German, Mandarin, Latin, etc.; world languages were listed as a shortage area in **35 states**. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4754/download?file=Teacher_Shortages_by_Subject_FACTSHEET.pdf&inline=&utm_source=openai))

5. **English as a Second Language / bilingual education**  
   Shortages are common where there are growing multilingual student populations. ESL was reported as a shortage area in **31 states**. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4754/download?file=Teacher_Shortages_by_Subject_FACTSHEET.pdf&inline=&utm_source=openai))

6. **Career and technical education — CTE**  
   This includes areas like agriculture, construction trades, health sciences, business, computer science, engineering/technology, culinary arts, automotive, and manufacturing. CTE was reported as a shortage area in **33 states**. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4754/download?file=Teacher_Shortages_by_Subject_FACTSHEET.pdf&inline=&utm_source=openai))

7. **Computer science**  
   This is often a shortage because people with CS skills can earn more outside education, and some districts—especially rural or under-resourced ones—struggle to offer CS classes due to lack of certified/experienced teachers. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17483?utm_source=openai))

A useful shorthand is: **special education, math, science, ESL/bilingual, world languages, and CTE/computer science** are the safest bets if you’re asking “where are teachers most needed?”

That said, there may be **less shortage or even competition** in fields like social studies, elementary education, English/language arts, art, music, and PE—though this varies widely by location. A “teacher shortage” is rarely universal; it is usually a **shortage of specific certified teachers in specific places**.
